title: CREATING, VIEWING, AND EDITING TEXT FILES
display: Ch 5 — CREATING, VIEWING, AND EDITING TEXT FILES

content.text: Book reference: Chapter 5, pages 125–159. Guided Exercises: Editing Text Files from the Shell Prompt, Changing the Shell Environment. Lab: Creating, Viewing, and Editing Text Files.
RHCSA EXAM CRITICAL — This whole chapter

Vim is how you'll edit every configuration file on the RHCSA exam — there's no guaranteed graphical editor. Redirection and pipes are how you'll capture command output as proof of work and feed one command's results into another. Budget real practice time here.
Every process starts with three numbered communication channels ("file descriptors"):
| # | Name | Default connection |
| 0 | stdin (standard input) | Keyboard |
| 1 | stdout (standard output) | Terminal |
| 2 | stderr (standard error) | Terminal |

Redirection swaps a file in for the keyboard/terminal on either end. This is exactly why redirecting stdout alone doesn't hide error messages — they travel on channel 2, a separate pipe entirely, and keep going to your screen unless you redirect that too.
| Operator | Effect |
| `> file` | stdout overwrites file (creates it if missing) |
| `>> file` | stdout appends to file |
| `2> file` | stderr overwrites file |
| `2> /dev/null` | discard error messages entirely |
| `> file 2>&1` | stdout AND stderr both to file (order matters — see below) |
| `&> file` | same as above, shorter modern syntax |
| `&>> file` | stdout AND stderr both appended to file |
WARNING — Order matters with 2>&1
> file 2>&1 means "send stdout to file, then point stderr at wherever stdout is now pointing" — both end up in file. Correct.

2>&1 > file means "point stderr at wherever stdout currently is (the terminal), then send stdout to file" — stderr still prints to your screen. This is a classic mistake; the merging operators &> and &>> sidestep the ordering trap entirely, which is why many admins prefer them, though some scripting purists avoid them for portability to non-bash shells. Both styles are common in the field — know both.
date > /tmp/saved-timestamp # save output
find /etc -name passwd 2> /tmp/errors # errors only to file, output stays on screen
find /etc -name passwd > /tmp/out 2> /tmp/errors # split output and errors into two files
find /etc -name passwd &> /tmp/both # both together
find /etc -name passwd > /tmp/out 2> /dev/null # keep output, throw errors away
| connects one command's stdout directly to the next command's stdin — no file touches disk in between.
ls -l /usr/bin | less # page through long output
ls | wc -l # count how many files are in the current directory
ls -t | head -n 10 > recent.txt # newest 10 files, saved to a file
RHCSA EXAM CRITICAL — tee — save AND view at the same time

Putting > file in the middle of a pipeline sends output only to that file — nothing reaches the next command, which is rarely what you want. tee solves this: it copies its input to a file while also passing it straight through to stdout, so the pipeline keeps flowing.
ls -l | tee /tmp/saved-output | less # saved to file AND shown on screen
One exception: &> and &>> cannot be used to pipe stderr — for that, put 2>&1 before the pipe: find / -name passwd 2>&1 | less.

Every RHEL system ships at least a minimal vi; most also have vim-enhanced, which upgrades the plain vi command to full Vim automatically for regular users (root and other low-UID system accounts are deliberately excluded from that alias, so vi still means plain vi for root unless you type vim explicitly).
💡 Why this matters — Why Vim specifically, out of every editor that exists

vi is required by the POSIX standard, so some form of it is essentially guaranteed on any Linux/UNIX-like box you'll ever touch — including macOS. Learning it once means you're never stuck without an editor on an unfamiliar server, which is exactly the scenario the RHCSA exam is testing for.
The three modes that matter
| Mode | Enter with | Purpose |
| Command mode | (default on open, or `Esc` from elsewhere) | Navigation, delete, copy/paste, undo |
| Insert mode | `i` | Typing becomes file content |
| Extended command mode | `:` | Save, quit, search/replace, and other whole-file operations |
NOTE — Lost? Press Esc
If you're not sure what mode you're in, pressing Esc repeatedly is always safe and gets you back to command mode — it does nothing harmful if you're already there.
The minimum survival command set
| Keys | Effect |
| `i` | Enter insert mode at the cursor |
| `Esc` | Leave insert mode, back to command mode |
| `x` | Delete the character under the cursor |
| `u` | Undo the last change |
| `:w` | Write (save), stay open |
| `:wq` | Write and quit |
| `:q!` | Quit, discarding changes since the last save |
RHCSA EXAM CRITICAL — This table is exam-day muscle memory
If you only memorize seven Vim keystrokes for the whole course, memorize these seven — every config-file edit on the exam runs through this exact set.
Copy/paste and visual mode
Vim calls copy/paste "yank and put": y yanks a visual-mode selection into memory, p puts it at the cursor. Visual mode itself has three flavors:
| Key | Selects |
| `v` | Character by character |
| `Shift+V` | Whole lines |
| `Ctrl+V` | A rectangular block — ideal for editing a column across many lines at once |
Practice these hands-on with the built-in tutorial, which ships with vim-enhanced:
vimtutor
VARNAME=value sets a shell variable — letters, digits, and underscore only in the name. It exists only in that one shell session; a second terminal or SSH login won't see it.
COUNT=40
echo $COUNT # → 40
echo ${COUNT}x # braces protect the name when characters follow it directly
WARNING — Bare variable name vs. $-prefixed
echo COUNT prints the literal word "COUNT". echo $COUNT prints its value. This trips up almost everyone at least once.
Shell variables you'll actually touch
| Variable | Controls |
| `PS1` | The prompt's appearance — e.g. `PS1='[\u@\h \t \w]$ '` adds user, host, time, working dir. |
| `HISTFILE` / `HISTFILESIZE` | Where shell history is saved (default `~/.bash_history`) and how many commands it keeps. |
Quoting rule: any value containing a space (like a PS1 string) must be quoted, single or double — this is not optional, and the recommended style also ends PS1 with a trailing space for readability.
Turning a shell variable into an environment variable
Plain shell variables are invisible to programs you launch. export promotes one to an environment variable, which every child process inherits:
export EDITOR=vim # set and export in one step
echo $PATH # colon-separated list the shell searches, in order, for a command's executable
| Variable | Meaning |
| `PATH` | Directories searched (in order) to find a command's executable |
| `HOME` | Your home directory — set automatically at shell start |
| `EDITOR` | Default command-line editor many programs invoke |
| `LANG` | Locale — language, character set, date/number formatting |
💡 Why this matters — Why PS1 and HISTFILE never get exported

Only the shell itself reads those two — no external program needs them — so exporting them would accomplish nothing. PATH, EDITOR, and LANG matter precisely because other programs (not just the shell) read them, which is the entire purpose of export.

env lists every environment variable currently set. unset VARNAME removes a variable entirely; export -n VARNAME keeps the variable but un-exports it (the shell keeps it, child programs stop seeing it).
Making it permanent: Bash startup files
Variables set directly at the prompt vanish when that shell exits. To make a setting stick for every future login, put it in a startup file instead:
| Scope | Edit this file |
| Just your account, every interactive shell | `~/.bashrc` |
| Every account on the system | A new `.sh` file in `/etc/profile.d/` (root required) |
# added to ~/.bashrc:
export EDITOR=nano
RHCSA EXAM CRITICAL — Persisting PS1 in the lab

Editing ~/.bashrc to add a PS1 line, then logging out and back in to confirm it took effect, is precisely the kind of task-plus-verification pattern the exam rewards — don't just make a change, prove it worked.

sections.title: Hands-on: practice these on your own lab

content.text: 1. find /etc -name '*.conf' > /tmp/out 2> /tmp/errors — inspect both files afterward with less.
2. ls -l /etc | tee /tmp/etc-listing | wc -l — confirm the file was written AND the count printed.
3. vim ~/practice.txt — type a few lines in insert mode, Esc, then :wq. Reopen it with vim to confirm it saved.
4. In vim, select three lines with Shift+V, y to yank, move the cursor, p to put — confirm the copy.
5. export GREETING="hello lab"; echo $GREETING, then open a second SSH session to the same box and echo $GREETING again — confirm it's empty there, proving variables are per-session.
6. Add export EDITOR=vim to ~/.bashrc, log out, log back in, then echo $EDITOR to confirm it persisted.
1. Q1 — Write a single command that runs a find command, keeps normal output on the screen, but throws away only the error messages.
2. Q2 — You run somecommand > out.txt | less and out.txt fills up but less shows nothing. Why, and what command fixes it while keeping both behaviors?
3. Q3 — You're mid-edit in vim and can't remember if you're in insert or command mode. What's the safe move, and why is it safe?
NOTE — Answers
Q1 — find /some/path 2> /dev/null (redirect only channel 2 to the null device; stdout is untouched and still prints).

Q2 — Redirection is set up before the pipe connects, so > out.txt claims all of stdout for the file and nothing is left to flow into less. Fix: tee — somecommand | tee out.txt | less sends output both to the file and onward through the pipe.
Q3 — Press Esc. In command mode Esc does nothing harmful, and from insert mode it simply exits to command mode — so pressing it (even repeatedly, even if you're unsure) can never make things worse.
- Every process has stdin/stdout/stderr on channels 0/1/2; redirecting one doesn't affect the others unless you explicitly merge them (2>&1, &>).
- Pipes (|) connect commands directly; tee lets you save to a file and keep the pipeline flowing at the same time.
- Vim's three core modes are command, insert (i), and extended command (:) — i / Esc / x / u / :w / :wq / :q! covers the exam-critical minimum.
- Shell variables live in one session only; export promotes one to an environment variable that child processes inherit.
- ~/.bashrc makes a setting persistent for your account; /etc/profile.d/*.sh makes it system-wide.
